items.title: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job?
items.summary:
The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration

Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes.

This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words.

Continue reading...

items.title: ‘Absurd’: Delta CEO says it takes longer to fly from ATL to LGA today than in the 1950s
items.summary:
Delta CEO Ed Bastian says one of his airline’s oldest routes is slower now than when it launched in the 1950s, and it’s “absurd.”

“Today, it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd,” Bastian told Fortune’ s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum on Monday. 

His complaint lands days after the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide grounding of flights last week put the country’s congested air traffic control system back in the spotlight. Bastian said fixing it would bring ticket prices down by letting airlines add flights, but modernization can’t happen without investment, which doesn’t seem likely when the data-center buildout is diverting trillions in capital. 

“We can’t even get $50 billion to fix our skies, which affects all of us at a much higher level than any individual data center,” Bastian said. 

Airplanes have become more advanced since the one equipped for the world’s first scheduled commercial flight from St. Petersburg to Tampa over a century ago . By Bastian’s account, the system they fly through hasn’t kept up.

Delta is also grappling with airfare pricing after the Iran war’s pressure on jet fuel prices squeezed the airline industry , and it has passed much of that cost onto consumers. Bastian said Delta’s tickets are 15% to 20% higher year-over-year because of jet fuel, adding that this wouldn’t have been possible to do if there wasn’t sufficient demand.

“We would not be able to generate that type of pricing if we didn’t have a consumer that was…

items.summary:
When Anthropic goes public this week, several big players will enjoy a windfall after having snapped up shares at firesale prices in 2024 at the bankruptcy liquidation of collapsed crypto exchange FTX. Those include the quant giant Jane Street, which spent $1.34 billion to purchase Anthropic shares at the time—a stake that is likely to be worth over $35 million after the IPO. And, in a twist of fate, Jane Street is the first employer of Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced founder of FTX, who is now serving a 25-year sentence for fraud in federal prison.

Bankman-Fried expressed frustration over the sale in a recent interview with The New York Times , criticizing the bankruptcy administrators who took control of FTX after its collapse. In addition to Jane Street, other buyers of FTX’s Anthropic shares are an investment vehicle linked to Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala and the Ford Foundation, both of which are also poised to share in the windfall.

Bankman-Fried became one of Anthropic’s earliest investors in late 2021, when he put $500 million into the little-known startup for a 13.5% stake that later shrank as the company raised more money, according to The New York Times .

Nearly five years later, Anthropic is just two days away from pricing what could be one of the largest initial public offerings in history, with trading on the Nasdaq expected to begin Thursday. Its proposed price range of $70 to $78 per share would value the company at up to roughly $1.4 trillion . items.title: At 17, South Carolina-bound GG Banks is building a brand before her first college game
items.summary:
Jezelle “GG” Banks doesn’t turn 18 until Nov. 27, but she already has a logo.

The senior at The St. James Academy, just outside Washington, D.C., is a five-star guard ranked No. 4 in the class of 2027 and committed to South Carolina, the No. 1 team in the AP poll. She’s as at home slicing past defenders as she is hosting long livestreams on social media.

Banks is also building a business. In a growing number of states, high school athletes can now be paid for their name, image, and likeness (NIL), just like college athletes. In an exclusive interview with Fortune , she revealed her personal logo publicly for the first time.

“I love it! It really fits me,” Banks said. “Everything in the logo has special meaning to me. I think the logo speaks to my personality—spikes of energy boosting everything, and then towards the bottom you’ve got a dollar sign, because, of course, banks.”

Dominique Oliveto 

The dollar sign plays on her last name. Banks worked on the design with her agency, THE·TEAM , the sports and entertainment firm formerly known as Wasserman. Coming just weeks before her 18th birthday, it’s a birthday present of sorts.

“This was a dream,” Banks said. THE·TEAM showed her mockups of the logo on sneakers and in Times Square. “That’s what I envisioned when I was younger, me having the logo.”

Building who she was on the court 

Custom logos are still rare among high school players, but Banks has been dreaming big for a while.

“I saw this coming a little bit, not just for me, but I think just the women’s era—people paying more attention to women’s basketball,” she…

items.title: The Nvidia scandal fuels tougher China chip rules as Commerce targets Singapore and Malaysia
items.summary:
When Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday , critics of the U.S.’s policy of restricting chip sales to China lost one of their biggest allies.

In addition to being one of the industry’s biggest proponents of the AI buildout, Huang remains one of the most vocal critics of U.S. policies that bar the sale of advanced chips and chipmaking equipment to China. He claimed that these measures would encourage the creation of a competing Chinese chip industry, and that it was better for the U.S. to keep Chinese companies hooked on U.S. technology. 

Nvidia’s CEO was also a strong supporter of open-source AI models—many of which came from Chinese developers like DeepSeek—in the face of criticism that such models posed a serious cybersecurity threat. 

Revelations that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation)—a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean company suspected of funnelling controlled chips to China—has torched the Nvidia CEO’s credibility on the issue of export controls. (Some reports claim U.S. intelligence considered Alice Huang to be part of a Chinese espionage campaign against Nvidia, but others have cast doubt on that assessment).

On Monday morning, the U.S. Department of Commerce released the first update to its export control regime since the scandal broke, issuing an interim final rule that closes a longstanding loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access AI chips based in overseas data centers, and expands export controls to an array of Southeast Asian countries. Congress, too, is debating several laws that would codify and expand…

items.title: ‘Steve Jobs ruined everything with the iPhone’: Tech billionaire Palmer Luckey gets real on what really killed the 10,000-hour rule
items.summary:
Palmer Luckey has a complaint about the iPhone, and he took it to Steve Jobs’s biographer.

“Steve Jobs ruined everything with the iPhone,” Luckey, the Oculus inventor and Anduril cofounder, tells Walter Isaacson in an episode of Isaacson’s podcast The Builders airing Tuesday, an excerpt of which was shared exclusively with Fortune . “We’re still suffering the impacts of his incredible product design.”

Luckey, worth an estimated $5.9 billion according to Forbes , offered an argument about skill: the iPhone made technology so easy to learn that there’s nothing left to get good at, and every product since has copied it. Luckey founded Oculus in 2012, and Facebook bought it in 2014 for more than $2 billion. He left in 2017 to found Anduril, a defense company last valued at $61 billion. Last year, Anduril and Meta teamed up to build augmented- and virtual-reality gear for the U.S. Army, and Luckey recently partnered with the dire wolf and woolly mammoth-cloning entrepreneur Ben Lamm to breed genetically engineered clone dogs for military use, via a company called Warhound .

The 10-minute ceiling 

Isaacson opened with a theory that the greatest advances in tech come at the human-machine interface, from Doug Engelbart’s mouse through the graphical interface and Jobs, “maybe culminating with Neuralink and chips in our brain.”

Before the iPhone, Luckey responded, “there was an understanding that technology was something that could multiply your output.” He pointed to Jobs’s own line about the computer as a “ bicycle for the mind .” But the iPhone turned out to be a…

items.summary:
Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian thinks Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop came from “a combination of faulty equipment, coupled with human error.” He dismissed other explanations as currently lacking evidence. “There’s no evidence that there’s [an] AI trigger. There’s no evidence that there’s cyber at play.”

Bastian, speaking with Fortune’ s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, said he has no information beyond what has been reported. “We’ll find out when it comes in,” he said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, canceling roughly 12,500 flights that day and thousands more on Saturday. It was the first nationwide stop since a January 2023 system outage, and only the second since 9/11.

What led to the FAA ground stop 

Bastian said he has talked to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, and that Duffy “has been very transparent.” Duffy has said the trouble started during a copper-to-fiber switch at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Ark. A router at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, then “started to flood our system.” Contractor L3Harris did the installation, and Duffy has asked publicly whether the fault was the install or the router itself. L3Harris says it is supporting the investigation. Bedford said there was “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related.”

items.title: Don’t just use AI to cut costs. Use it to create growth
items.summary:
Every CEO I talk to has an AI savings plan. Almost none have an AI revenue plan.

Savings matter. But an AI strategy that stops there is incomplete.

Across 50 years of entrepreneurship, I’ve helped create more than 175 companies. I’ve watched successive technology waves play out the same way. The first instinct is to use the new tool to do the old things cheaper. The companies that win use it to do new things. Electricity didn’t just lower factory power bills; it let factories be rebuilt around the assembly line. The internet didn’t just cut the cost of mailing catalogs; it created Amazon .

An EY-Parthenon survey published in April 2026 found that 63% of growth leaders at large U.S. companies said their organizations were using AI primarily for efficiency and productivity. Just 7% cited diversifying revenue streams. McKinsey’s 2026 research finds that AI high performers pursue growth or innovation alongside efficiency.

In a 2025 study of software and reasoning tasks, METR found that the length of tasks AI agents could complete with 50% reliability had been doubling roughly every seven months. Those lengths reflect how long the tasks take human experts.

AI is making ideas more abundant and early experimentation less expensive. For software-based concepts, it can help teams research a market, write and test code, and build an initial prototype before committing a larger team and budget. The hard part remains choosing the right opportunities, validating demand, and turning them into viable businesses. Established companies can draw on existing expertise and capabilities…
items.t: Don’t just use AI to cut costs. Use it to create growth

items.title: South Korea faces an AI cheating scandal days before its national college entrance exams
items.summary:
South Korea’s top scorer on the national tax accountant qualification exam has admitted to using AI to cheat. 

Han Won-seok revealed in a video posted on his lawyer’s YouTube channel that he used a small camera to photograph exam questions, sent the images to an AI tool, and checked the answers on his smartphone. He wore a face mask in the 14-minute long video, which has garnered more than 1.5 million views since being posted on Nov. 15. 

The Ministry of Economy and Finance will move to suspend Han’s qualifications. Under Korean law, candidates that cheat on their exam results are barred from taking the test again for five years, according to the Korea Herald. 

South Korea’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin said during a committee meeting on Monday that the ministry would inspect every pair of glasses worn by students during this week’s national college entrance exams. Reuters reported that smart devices were added to a list of banned items in July. 

Han acknowledged that his top ranking was fraudulent and apologized to fellow candidates, tax professionals, and exam officials. He also admitted to using the same method to cheat on a separate certified public accountant exam. “I deeply regret what I did,” Han said. 

Han said he is cooperating with authorities and would turn over his electronic equipment. He said he hoped an investigation might prevent similar incidents. 

Asked by his lawyer why he cheated, Han said he was worried about his future and wanted to make his parents proud. He said he later felt overwhelmed by guilt, particularly toward the runner up.

items.title: ‘The currency competition is now a software competition’: Why Japan’s banks think digital currencies give the yen a boost
items.summary:
Currencies such as the Japanese yen or the euro have tried and failed to loosen the U.S. dollar’s grip on world trade , unable to outweigh the U.S.’s deep and open financial markets. But now, Japanese bankers think that the rise of digital currencies could give the yen a new path to worldwide use.

“The currency competition is now a software competition,” Tomoya Hasebe, global head of digital and innovation at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), said at a roundtable organized by FinCity Tokyo in Singapore on Nov. 16. “Currency dominance is increasingly determined not only by central bank policy or regulatory policy, but by which currency is easiest to use as code.” 

The yen is the world’s third most-used currency, after the U.S. dollar and the euro.

Japan was the first country among G7 economies to roll out a comprehensive framework to regulate stablecoins. Yet yen-pegged stablecoins have barely enjoyed much usage, with U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins accounting for more than 97% of the market .

The country’s three megabanks— Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group, and the Mizuho Financial Group—are planning to change that with a jointly-issued yen-backed stablecoin set to begin transactions next March . The new stablecoin is meant to streamline cross-border payments and boost the appeal of the yen for global business.

Several Asian economies are rolling out their own stablecoins to cater to firms seeking alternatives to the U.S. dollar. Hong Kong, for example, issued its first two Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin issuer licenses…
items.t: ‘The currency competition is now a software competition’: Why Japan’s banks think digital currencies give the yen a boost

The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. items.title: ‘Shameless venality’: how a flurry of lawsuits has thwarted Trump’s self-enrichment schemes
items.summary:
Courts have issued stinging rebukes to president’s ‘blatant’ financial ploys as pro-democracy groups defend ‘government of laws, not of men’ pillar

Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys to increase his wealth and boost Republican electoral prospects have fueled lawsuits by non-partisan groups, prompting federal judges to issue stinging rejections to some of the president’s schemes.

Several lawsuits were filed in 2026 against Trump’s schemes to benefit his bottom line by reducing potential tax liabilities, boosting his Truth Social platform financially by offering big investors early access to his posts, and helping Republicans by using federal funds to pay for highly partisan ads touting Trump’s record in the run-up to the midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered a heavy defeat.

But as the notes of cinnamon and clove fill the room will you be burning money spent on the White Company’s £95 “winter indulgence” candle that customers describe as the “scent of Christmas”. Or have you followed TikTok’s advice and bought the Aldi “dupe” for £25.

items.title: Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream? | John Harris
items.summary:
Nearly 2 million children are housed in dire conditions, anxious families are living out of carrier bags. There’s little sign of the hope our PM promised

Two days after the Christmas of 2024, Andy Burnham put up a post on X that linked to a piece about housing in the Guardian. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, who was beginning to find his voice as a frank critic of Keir Starmer’s new government, did not mess about: “The Government should make building hundreds of thousands of council homes its defining purpose,” he said. “No other policy, achievable within a parliament, would have greater social and economic benefits.”

In his first Labour conference speech as party leader and prime minister, Burnham reprised much the same argument, promising “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar era”. But by that point, he had also served notice that his commitment to a thoroughgoing council house revival might not be quite as cast iron as it seemed. The previous month, having insisted that all of the £39bn Rachel Reeves had promised to spend on the Starmer government’s Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) until 2036 should go on homes for social rent, he made something of a brazen U-turn, announcing that the allocation of the first £10bn would reflect the existing social…

A head of steam is building up behind the Bank of England raising interest rates again. With the latest forecasts by the central bank showing inflation rising to 5% next spring, another increase in the cost of borrowing seems inevitable, and may come as soon as next month.

A growing number of analysts predict the Bank’s policymakers will don Scrooge masks when they meet on 17 December to deliver a message of austerity and sacrifice.
